newsitem.title: JAPAN: Furukawa reveals plan to return to copper business.
newsitem.headline: Furukawa reveals plan to return to copper business.

text.p: Japan's oldest copper smelter Furukawa Co Ltd, which was forced to abandon production in the late 1980s, announced on Monday an ambitious plan to return to business -- not at home, but in Australia.
"We've been a pioneer in copper smelting here and provided other metal companies with technology for many years," Ichiro Fujimura, Furukawa's senior managing director, told Reuters.
"But currently we don't have our own smelting facility, and this is not an honourable situation for us," he said.
Furukawa and four other firms, including one Australian company, have agreed to form a copper smelting venture in New South Wales, Australia.

The other firms include Nissho Iwai Corp, Itochu Corp and Nittetsu Mining Co Ltd, Furukawa and the three Japanese companies said in a joint statement. The statement did not name the Australian partner.

It said the venture, to be called Port Kembla Copper Pty Ltd (PKC), would buy a copper smelting plant in Port Kembla, Wollongong, currently owned by Southern Copper Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Anglo-Australian mining giant RTZ Corp Plc -CRA Ltd.
PKC will be 50 percent owned by Furukawa, 20 percent by Nittetsu, 17.5 percent by Nissho Iwai and 10 percent by Itochu, it said.

The venture will renovate the plant so it can meet pollution regulations and boost its copper production capacity to 120,000 tonnes a year by the second half of 1998 from 80,000 tonnes currently, the statement said.
"Of the total production, we're going to export 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes of copper, particularly to Southeast Asia. We have no worry about sales," Furukawa's Fujimura told reporters.
Furukawa's copper smelting business dates as far back as 1878, when Japan was struggling to catch up with industrial powers like the United States and Britain.
Copper was then essential for the supply of electricity, and the Japanese government had provided Furukawa, founded by legendary businessman Ichibe Furukawa, with political and financial support.
But more than a century later, Furukawa was forced to abandon copper smelting in 1987 as the yen's steep climb against the dollar severely damaged the company's profitability.
"Our hope is to transfer Furukawa's sophisticated smelting technology overseas. This joint venture in Australia can be a first step in achieving that," a Furukawa official said.
The venture is considering further boosting the plant's capacity to 150,000 tonnes a year and aiming to boost sales in Asia as well as Australia, Furukawa said.
The Australian plant stopped operations at the end of 1994 as it needed funds to carry out modernisations to meet environmental regulations.
Furukawa said investment for the renovation and capacity increase was expected to total about A$250 million and operations at the plant were expected to begin in the second half of 1998.
